title: How University Disability Services Professionals Write Image Descriptions for HCI Figures Using Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university Disability Services Office (DSO) professionals write alternative text (alt text) for complex academic figures and whether generative AI can improve that process. The central problem is that accessibility professionals are often asked to describe figures from technical fields outside their expertise, which can lead to generic, incomplete, or inaccurate descriptions. The authors argue that this is especially problematic for screen reader users who rely on alt text to access visual information in academic materials.

The study evaluates a human-AI workflow using ChatGPT-4o as a writing assistant. In Study 1, 12 DSO professionals from higher education institutions wrote alt text for HCI publication figures both with and without AI assistance, while thinking aloud and completing interviews and questionnaires. The figures were selected from CHI 2025 papers and intentionally varied in complexity. In Study 2, 11 HCI experts evaluated the resulting alt texts using a rubric that assessed figure type identification, message, key elements, trends, clarity, detail, and contextual relevance. The design combines qualitative interview/thematic analysis with quantitative comparisons of confidence, text length, and rubric scores.

The participants were adults working in higher education accessibility roles, located in the United States, and the context was institutional accessibility remediation rather than K-12 instruction. The main findings are that AI assistance helped DSO professionals produce longer, faster, and higher-quality alt text, especially for complex figures, and increased their confidence. However, some participants over-relied on the AI, accepted outputs with insufficient checking, and struggled to prompt the model precisely. The evaluation by HCI experts found that AI-assisted alt text was generally superior to human-only alt text, though both approaches still showed weaknesses in specificity, clarity, and contextual accuracy.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot used for text and image understanding, drafting, and revising responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a writing assistant to generate and refine alt text for HCI figures written by DSO professionals; participants uploaded articles and figures and prompted the model to draft accessibility descriptions.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 with 12 DSO professionals, ChatGPT assistance helped participants write alt text more quickly and with less effort than writing without AI. All participants completed the AI-assisted writing task within 20 minutes, whereas without AI assistance all used the full 50 minutes and two could not complete descriptions of all figures.
findings.measure: Time to complete alt-text writing task; task completion

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated their confidence in AI-assisted alt text considerably higher than in self-written alt text. The paper also reports that ChatGPT-assisted descriptions were longer on average than human-only descriptions (mean=140.70 words, std=79.65 vs mean=104.16, std=66.21; t(36)=-2.09, p=0.044).
findings.measure: Perceived confidence in alt-text quality; alt-text word count

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 with 11 HCI experts, AI-assisted alt text was rated superior in quality to human-only alt text, even when some inaccuracies were present. The evaluation also found that human-generated alt text lacked specific details and was inconsistent.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods user study with expert evaluation, not a randomized controlled trial or meta-analysis. The paper provides descriptive and limited quantitative comparisons, so the evidence is useful but not high-credibility experimental evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects on efficiency, confidence, and expert-rated alt-text quality, but effect sizes are mostly not reported and the study is small. The overall impact appears promising but modest and context-specific.
